title: A SpaceX Rocket Crashed Into the Moon — and NASA Found the Hole!
summary:
Imagine a rocket the size of a school bus flying through space for over a year. Then, WHAM! It crashes into the moon at 5,400 miles per hour. That's way faster than any airplane. This happened on August 5, and now NASA has pictures of the crash site.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has been circling the moon for years, taking photos. It snapped pictures of the new crater on August 11 and 12. The crater is about 60 feet wide — that's as long as two school buses parked end to end. It's not very deep, less than 10 feet.

The crater looks like a big splash. There are bright and dark streaks shooting out from it. The dark streaks are old moon dust that got tossed up. The bright streaks are fresh rock from underground. Scientists say the shape of the splash shows the rocket hit at a low angle, like a stone skipping across water.

The rocket was a Falcon 9 upper stage from SpaceX. It had been floating in space for over a year and a half. It was leftover from a mission that sent two robotic landers to the moon in January 2025. One lander, Blue Ghost, landed safely. The other one, Resilience, crashed. Now the rocket that carried them is also a moon crater.

Another spacecraft, from South Korea, also saw the crater first. It's called Danuri. Danuri sent the exact location to NASA so LRO could take better pictures. Scientists will keep studying the crater to learn more about what happens when things hit the moon. Maybe one day, astronauts will visit it!
why_it_matters: Leftover space junk can affect other worlds, and learning from this crash may help scientists protect future moon missions.

background_read: NASA is the U.S. space agency; its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has been circling the moon and taking photos for years.
SpaceX is an American rocket company whose Falcon 9 rockets carry satellites and landers into space.
South Korea's Danuri is a moon orbiter, a spacecraft that circles the moon and takes its own measurements.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the crash site after South Korea's Danuri spacecraft found its exact location.
WHAT: A leftover SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage crashed into the moon at 5,400 miles per hour and blasted a crater about 60 feet wide.
WHERE: On the moon's surface, where the new crater is less than 10 feet deep and has bright and dark streaks around it.
WHY: Scientists are studying the splash shape and streaks to learn what happens when objects hit the moon at a low angle.

perspectives.description: They are glad to study a real crater and learn how a fast, low-angle impact throws old moon dust and fresh rock around.
They worry that leftover rocket parts can become dangerous litter, even far from Earth.
They want to use this information to make future moon landings safer and to understand the moon's surface.
